title: Checkpoint: How Weather Works
objective: After this level you can explain how heat, moisture, pressure and fronts combine to make the weather in your forecast.
summary: One storm ties the chapter together: a low steered by the jet stream brings a warm front's cirrus and rain, then a faster cold front's storms, sometimes an occlusion, then clear skies.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: one storm, from the first wisp to blue sky.
cards.body: A low-pressure system is heading your way. Follow it through and every idea from this chapter shows up, in order.

cards.headline: First: wisps, then gray
cards.body: The jet stream steers the low toward you from the west. Warm fronts often form on a low's east side, so the warm front arrives first. Warm air slides up over the cold air and cools to its dew point, so high cirrus appear, then lower, thicker cloud. Inside, ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled droplets, fall, and melt into rain.

cards.headline: Next: the cold front catches up
cards.body: Behind the low comes a cold front, moving up to twice as fast. Dense cold air shoves the warm air up, cumulonimbus tower, and thunderstorms roll through. Sometimes the cold front catches the warm front and lifts the warm air off the ground entirely. That's an occluded front, usually found near the center of the low.

cards.fact: After a cold front passes, pressure starts rising and the skies clear.
cards.context: Cooler air takes over. If a high builds in behind it, sinking air holds back the clouds and settled weather follows. Weather is air masses taking turns, and fronts are the handovers.

mascot.line: That's the whole chapter in one storm. If you can narrate this forecast, you've got How Weather Works.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: How rising air cools to its dew point and turns invisible vapor into clouds and rain.
Why most rain outside the tropics starts as snow, while warm tropical clouds rain without ice.
What highs, lows, air masses and fronts each do to the weather in your forecast.
How three circulation cells and the jet stream steer storms around the planet.

options.label: A front that has stopped moving
A warm front that has caught up with a cold front
options.rationale: It's the other way around; cold fronts are faster.

options.label: A cold front that has caught up with a warm front
The boundary around a high-pressure system
options.rationale: Fronts separate air masses; highs don't have one around them.

questions.explanation: Cold fronts move faster, so a cold front can catch the warm front ahead of it and lift the warm air off the ground: an occluded front.

questions.prompt: Why can a cold front catch up with the warm front ahead of it?

options.label: Cold fronts move up to twice as fast
Warm fronts stop moving at night
options.rationale: Warm fronts are slow, but they don't stop at night.

options.label: The jet stream blows warm fronts backward
options.rationale: The jet steers the whole low forward.

options.label: Cold air rises over warm air and overtakes it
options.rationale: Cold air pushes under warm air, not over it.

questions.explanation: Warm air struggles to push dense cold air aside, so warm fronts crawl; cold fronts move up to twice as fast and can overtake them.

questions.prompt: The warm front's rain began as ice. How did the ice crystals grow?

options.label: By freezing onto specks of sea salt
options.rationale: Salt helps droplets form, but the ice grows from vapor.

options.label: By colliding with warm raindrops
options.rationale: Collisions are the warm-cloud process of the tropics.

options.label: By melting and refreezing again and again
options.rationale: Melting comes at the end, below the cloud.

options.label: By taking water vapor as supercooled droplets evaporated

questions.explanation: In the Bergeron process, vapor deposits onto ice more readily than onto liquid, so ice crystals grow while supercooled droplets evaporate.

questions.prompt: What steers a low-pressure system across the map?

options.label: The Intertropical Convergence Zone
options.rationale: The ITCZ is a stormy belt near the Equator.

options.label: The dew point
options.rationale: The dew point is a temperature, not a wind.

options.label: Condensation nuclei
options.rationale: Those are specks that help droplets form.

questions.explanation: Jet streams carry weather systems along; the polar front jet steers lows, usually from west to east.

questions.prompt: Put what you see as the storm passes in order.
questions.explanation: High cirrus appear, then lower, thicker cloud brings rain. The cold front follows and thunderstorms roll through, then the skies clear.
